question:
Patient note:
A 58-year-old woman is evaluated in the pre-operative bay just before transfer to the operating theatre for an elective four-port laparoscopic fundoplication to treat long-standing, proton-pump-inhibitor-refractory gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. She walked from the visitor garage unaided, climbed a flight of stairs to registration, and has spent the morning seated in the waiting room reading the newspaper, reporting that she continues to manage household chores, garden for an hour most afternoons, and complete a two-kilometre stroll after dinner with her spouse; thus her baseline activity remains intact. The forthcoming procedure will be her first in more than a decade, and she confirms that she has not undergone any operation or endoscopic intervention in the past four weeks. Review of her recent medical course reveals that twenty-one days ago she awoke with transient slurred speech and mild facial droop; brain MRI demonstrated a small right pontine diffusion-positive lesion without large-vessel occlusion, and her deficits resolved within forty-eight hours after antiplatelet therapy was started. She required no thrombolysis, mechanical thrombectomy, or rehabilitation stay and was discharged home on day three with favourable neurologic examination. No additional cerebrovascular events have occurred since, but the episode places today’s surgery within the thirty-day window of an ischaemic stroke. Past medical history is also notable for moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease attributed to a forty-pack-year smoking history; she quit twelve years ago and now uses a tiotropium inhaler each morning plus salbutamol as needed, reporting one mild exacerbation last winter that was managed in the outpatient setting. She denies any history of systolic dysfunction, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, peripheral oedema, or prior echocardiograms suggesting reduced ejection fraction. There have been no recent chest infections, and she has been afebrile with stable respiratory symptoms over the past several months. Skeletal integrity has been intact: she has never fractured her hip, pelvis, or long bones, never worn a cast or brace, and has suffered no multi-system trauma. She has not been confined to bed for any reason and remains fully ambulatory at home and in the community. Vascular access consists only of a single 18-gauge peripheral cannula placed this morning in the left dorsum of the hand; she has never had a peripherally inserted central catheter, chemo port, or tunnelled dialysis line. Examination of the lower limbs shows equal calf circumferences, warm skin, easily compressible pretibial tissue without pitting, and an absence of tortuous superficial channels. She recalls no episodes of spontaneous leg swelling, pleuritic chest pain, or imaging-confirmed venous or pulmonary clot, and there is no family lore of thrombotic disease in first-degree relatives. Nevertheless, five years ago a haematology consultation for mildly prolonged prothrombin time uncovered heterozygosity for the G20210A mutation in the prothrombin gene; lifelong anticoagulation was not advised given the absence of clinical thrombosis, but the finding is documented on her problem list. Serologic testing at that time was negative for factor V Leiden, lupus anticoagulant, or anticardiolipin antibody, and homocysteine concentration was within reference limits. She carries no diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease, malignancy, myocardial infarction, connective-tissue disorder, or endocrine abnormality, and her only chronic medications are omeprazole 40 mg twice daily for reflux, tiotropium 18 µg inhaled once daily, salbutamol 100 µg two puffs as needed (last use three days ago), low-dose aspirin started after the recent pontine infarct, and cholecalciferol 1000 IU daily. She abstains from alcohol, denies illicit drug use, and has maintained a body mass index of 29 kg m⁻². On arrival her vital signs were temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 126/74 mm Hg, heart rate 72 beats min⁻¹ regular, respiratory rate 14 min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 96 % breathing ambient air. Airway evaluation reveals a Mallampati class II view, full cervical range of motion, three-finger thyro-mental distance, and secure dentition. Jugular venous pressure is not elevated, cardiac auscultation discloses crisp S₁ and S₂ without murmurs or gallops, and peripheral pulses are 2+ bilaterally. Lungs exhibit scattered end-expiratory wheezes that clear with forced exhalation and no crackles. Abdomen is soft and non-tender with mild epigastric fullness but no organomegaly. Neurological screening confirms intact cranial nerves, symmetric strength in all extremities, normal heel-to-shin testing, and no residual facial weakness or dysarthria. Laboratory studies drawn two hours ago show haemoglobin 13.2 g dL⁻¹, platelet count 210 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, leukocytes 7.1 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, sodium 139 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.1 mmol L⁻¹, creatinine 0.84 mg dL⁻¹, AST 20 U L⁻¹, ALT 24 U L⁻¹, total bilirubin 0.7 mg dL⁻¹, and international normalised ratio 1.1, consistent with prior results; activated partial thromboplastin time is 31 s. Twelve-lead ECG shows normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats min⁻¹ with preserved intervals and no acute ST–T changes. A screening chest radiograph obtained yesterday depicts hyperinflated lung fields without infiltrate and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette. Sequential pneumatic compression devices are stationed at the foot of the stretcher to be fitted after induction, and no pharmacologic thromboprophylaxis has yet been delivered in keeping with institutional policy to dose after port placement. She has been nil per os since midnight, last voided one hour ago, and expresses understanding of the operative plan, anaesthetic approach, and anticipated overnight stay for observation of respiratory status and post-stroke neurological monitoring.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini VTE score adds weighted patient and procedure risk factors:
- Age 41–60: age 58 = 1.
- BMI >25 kg/m²: BMI 29 = 1.
- Chronic lung disease: COPD = 1.
- Laparoscopic surgery lasting >45 minutes: assuming the planned fundoplication will exceed this threshold = 2. Duration is not explicitly stated.
- Documented thrombophilia: prothrombin G20210A mutation = 3, even without a prior clot.
- Stroke within one month: MRI-confirmed pontine infarct 21 days ago = 5, despite neurologic recovery.
No additional points are documented for immobility, venous access (the cannula is peripheral), prior VTE, or other risk factors. Sum: 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 5 = 13.
Final answer: 13
